title: Nubya Garcia - Breaking and Entering
summary: Nubya Garcia talks to Simon Winkler and Lauren Taylor on Breaking and Entering
transcript:
Nubya Garcia, the London-based tenor saxophonist, composer and bandleader, joined Lauren Taylor and Simon Winkler in the Triple R studios on 7 June 2018. She was in Melbourne for her Australian debut at The Jazzlab during the Melbourne International Jazz Festival, with two sold-out shows that evening. Edited for length and clarity.

Lauren: Welcome to Australia as well. It’s your Australian debut show tonight.

Nubya: Yeah, it’s quite mad. We’ve been here for less than 24 hours. But it feels really good to be here and I’m really looking forward to tonight. I can’t really believe it’s happening.

Lauren: You’re playing at The Jazzlab as part of the Melbourne International Jazz Festival. I think the seven o’clock show is sold out tonight, but you’re doing another show.

Nubya: I think they’re both sold out. So thank you to everyone who bought a ticket.

Lauren: You started playing music at the age of five and played a number of instruments, including, I think, the violin. Do you remember when you were first introduced to your instrument of choice, the saxophone?

Nubya: Music’s been around in my family for as long as I can remember. I’m the youngest of four, and my eldest sister’s 10 years older than me. I’ve got two sisters and a brother that are older than me, and they went to music stuff on the weekend, music classes. I literally don’t remember a time where I wasn’t going to pick them up or with them or whatever. Then, lo and behold, I joined the fold, as you would say. But yeah, I got my first saxophone around the age of 10. Then that was that, really.

Simon: You grew up surrounded by siblings and family members who were deeply interested in music. Was there ever a time when you turned away from the soul and jazz you were surrounded by?

Nubya: I would say not the kind of jazz upbringing that I had. That was where I really found a home. But I was brought up in classical music, so that was definitely something that, rebel is the wrong word, but I don’t think it was my calling, let’s say. I enjoyed it. I had loads of friends that played classical music, playing in orchestras and stuff. It was a great hang, but musically, I know how much I enjoy playing this kind of music that I do, and my friends had that for classical music. When you get to a certain age, you’re just like, ‘I’m just not vibing off this as much, playing it.’ I can go and see their gigs and concerts and still really enjoy myself. But for me, I think maybe it could be a number of things. Maybe the instrument that I was playing, like classical saxophone, that’s what I did for years alongside the jazz. I also played the viola. Saxophone was the one for me, so I know that I didn’t really want to continue viola. When you know that, I think it’s quite hard to maintain it and keep your momentum up because you’re just like, ‘Well, I want to do this other instrument that I really enjoy.’

Lauren: Tomorrow’s Warriors is a community hub and an incubator for new talent that you were heavily involved with growing up, where you formed lifelong friendships. Can you tell us about it and how it assisted your development?

Nubya: Tomorrow’s Warriors are like the original saviours in so many ways. They, to this day, are supportive and encouraging and there. I think it’s so important to have mentors in your life, whatever area of your life it may be. Unbelievable thanks to Gary Crosby and Janine and Peter Edwards, Binker Golding, James McKay. I don’t want to leave anyone out. Nat Facey. These are all the mentors that we had.

In the groups that we were in, that’s where I met nearly everyone in my band currently. I met Moses there, Moses Boyd, obviously. I met Sheila Maurice-Grey there, Shirley Tetteh, Femi Koleoso, Joe Armon-Jones as well. I met him there. When I started going, there were small groups that met on the Saturday. We were just learning jazz standards and experimenting, playing music together and hanging out all weekend, which was wicked.

You’ve got your school friends, and it’s not a separation thing. At school loads of my friends played music, but there weren’t as many of us. The guys that I met in Tomorrow’s, it was just like this whole unit of everyone your age that is digging Sonny Rollins. It feels quite rare. It didn’t feel out of the norm because we were living in it, but we were just talking about so many different things at that time, as well as jazz. Skip forward a few years and we were going out to gigs together and different kinds of music. Then people started putting on their own gigs, forming bands. It’s just kind of snowballed from there. It’s been a very organic and natural process, but things would be very, very different if Gary and Janine and all of our mentors hadn’t educated and given us the place to grow. So endless, endless thank yous to Tomorrow’s Warriors family.

Simon: Improvisation is a key aspect of jazz in general. What form does it take in your own music and creative practice?

Nubya: Big question. It’s definitely at the forefront of the way I write and the way that I’ve been learning my instrument from the beginning. That was alongside reading for me. I went to jazz groups within Camden Music, one run by Nikki Yeoh, and she got me into this music. She introduced me to improvisation in such a positive way that is still with me till today. It’s an endless journey of discovery for me, and I hope it stays that way. I want to continue to learn. I want to continue to push myself. Improvisation completely pushes you and puts you in so many different situations.

Lauren: I always think it must be nice in a live show when you get to improvise, that it mixes things up for you every night.

Nubya: Yeah, it’s different every night. We’re on tour now. No gig will be the same. I really enjoy that, rather than playing exactly the same gig every night. That’s another way of doing things, and I’ve done that before and enjoyed it. But right now, within my music, it works much better. I feel more connected.

Simon: You’ve described one of your intentions in music as being for audiences to be present in the moment when you’re performing. Improvisation must require an extraordinary concentration on the present moment, to lock into what you’re thinking but also what other musicians are thinking. Can you elaborate on that mind state?

Nubya: It’s been on my mind for, I don’t know time-wise how long, but just in the reality that we all live in, we’re all plugged into screens and phones and stuff. Gigs are a wonderful opportunity to take the time to be in the room with however many people, whether it’s 10 or 2,000, and experience the same thing that you’re looking at and listening to, but getting different things out of it. That shared experience. I’m not a phone hater or anything on stage. I think phones and videos have helped get music to more people, absolutely, and share your experience another way. It’s just about realising that doing that for the whole gig, I feel like you put a barrier between you and whatever is going on, whatever you’re watching. It’s not just music, dance, it could be theatre, whatever genre. You don’t just hold your phone, you look at your phone to make sure you’re getting a crisp shot, do you know what I mean? When I was writing When We Are, it was just on my mind. I was thinking about it and so it came out in what I was trying to say.

It was just about being where you are when you’re there. Experiencing it and appreciating it. I’m definitely not against it because I do it. I just don’t do it as much as a lot of people.

Just recently, this is completely different, but a quick story. I was at Coachella a couple of months ago, saw the Beyoncé gig. I’m really small, so I was in the crowd and not that close, not too far, but I couldn’t see anything because all I could see was phones. I spent a large portion of the gig absolutely losing my mind, of course. But at the same time everyone around me would just have their hands in the air, consistently filming for the whole thing. Of course I got some videos. You switch off, I think, and you’re not experiencing it in the same way. Sharing is a beautiful thing. That was what was on my mind when I was discussing presence in my brain and what it means to live and be and connect to that, really.

Lauren: Someone you’ve worked with is Sam Shepherd, aka Floating Points. Can you tell us how that mentoring relationship formed?

Nubya: Time-wise, I don’t know, maybe it was one year, two years ago, maybe a year and a half, who knows. Basically, I won one of the Steve Reid InNOVAtion Awards, which is a partnership between the Steve Reid Foundation and Gilles Peterson and Brownswood and PRS Foundation. That involves mentorship for about a year, and you can do with that whatever you want. Basically, me and Sam just had a couple of sessions in the studio. I was like, ‘Can I just learn about some of the gear that you’ve got in your studio, some of the pedals that you have, whatever you’re using? Can you just tell me more about it?’ Looking into all the analogue synths that he has, that was mind-blowing. It was incredible. We talked about business stuff and I was just asking questions very casually. This was before I started my label and before I had recorded the last EP.

We were just having conversations, and he was on tour a lot, so when we did meet it was just to get as much information as I could. Then the next time, when I’d recorded everything, I took it to him and he gave me his opinion. I was like, ‘Look, I’m thinking about trying to involve electronics, but in remixes, not just live electronics.’ He recommended some people and gave me some ideas, and then we had a play and did some stuff. Hopefully when he’s back in town we’ll continue. It was just great to have someone that you look up to that you could just talk to about music, business and life. Also what he’s doing, learning about what he’s been up to is absolutely incredible. It was really valuable at the right time for me to be involved with that, and he’s an amazingly lovely guy as well, really supportive.

Simon: Thank you so much for being our guest on Breaking and Entering. All the best for the shows tonight. Then you’re off to Vivid Live in Sydney on the weekend as well.

Nubya: Yeah, we are. We’re at Castlemaine Jazz Festival tomorrow. There for a day or two and then back to Sydney, and then I come back to Melbourne after that. So thanks for having me.
